summary:
We developed LuminaLuna that is a free website and public API that shows, for any spot near the Moon's south pole and any hour from 2025 to 2030, whether a lander would have sunlight for solar power and a direct view of Earth for radio contact. Users can explore a polar map, open 23 candidate sites (including Artemis III regions) or click any point, compare sites side by side, and find the nearest nearby spot with a better view of Earth.

How it addresses the challenge: we turn real NASA data into clear answers. NASA LOLA laser terrain (80 m resolution) gives the full 360° horizon around each site, up to 300 km away. NASA JPL's DE421 ephemeris, checked against JPL Horizons, places the Sun and Earth every hour. Together they tell exactly when each is hidden behind the hills.

Why it is important: at the south pole the Sun and Earth stay very low, so a few kilometres can mean months of light or weeks of darkness and silence. Choosing the right site decides whether a mission has power and can talk to Earth, and LuminaLuna makes that choice visible to planners and students alike.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

LuminaLuna answers two questions for any spot near the Moon's south pole and any hour from 2025 to 2030: will a lander have sunlight for solar power, and will it see Earth for direct radio contact? Users can explore a polar map, open 23 candidate landing sites (including Artemis III regions) or click any point on the map, compare up to four sites side by side, and learn why the south pole is so difficult.

HOW IT WORKS

1. Terrain: we use NASA's LOLA laser altimetry maps (80 m resolution near the pole, 240 m further out). From each site we trace the horizon in 720 directions, up to 300 km away, including the curvature of the Moon.

2. Sun and Earth: NASA JPL's DE421 ephemeris gives their position every hour from 2025 to 2030. We checked it against JPL Horizons: the largest difference is 0.05 arc-seconds.

3. Visibility: for every hour we check whether at least half of the Sun's disk, and Earth, are above the hills. From that we compute the percentage of time in sunlight, the longest night, the time with Earth in view, the longest time without Earth, and the daily energy from a 1 m² solar panel.

4. Nearest spot that sees Earth: on any site's page, one click tests every point within 5 km and shows the closest one with a better view of Earth over the next 30 days, with its distance, direction and slope, so you know if a rover could get there.

All calculations run directly in the browser from pre-computed data, so the site is fast and works without a server. A public API returns the same results as JSON or CSV.

BENEFITS

- Real NASA data, not estimates: every number comes from measured terrain and official ephemerides.

- Hour-by-hour detail: not just yearly averages, but exactly when a site goes dark or loses contact with Earth, with countdowns to the next change.

- Any point, not only a fixed list: users can test their own location.

- Easy to understand: a Beginner mode in plain language, an Expert mode with angles and raw values, a 360° skyline view, and a Learn page.

- Open and reusable: free website, public API and downloadable results.

INTENDED IMPACT

Choosing a landing site at the south pole decides whether a mission has power and can talk to Earth. LuminaLuna helps mission planners make that choice quickly, helps students and the public understand why the south pole is so special, and gives other teams an open tool and API to build on.

TOOLS, LANGUAGES AND SOFTWARE

- Data: NASA LRO LOLA terrain maps, NASA JPL DE421 ephemeris, JPL Horizons for validation.

- Data pipeline: Python with NumPy, SciPy, rasterio, jplephem, SpiceyPy, Astropy, pandas and Matplotlib.

- API: Python with FastAPI and Uvicorn, tested with pytest, ready for Docker.

- Website: JavaScript, HTML, CSS and SVG, with no framework; hosted on GitHub Pages.

- Design and testing: Google Stitch for mockups, Playwright for automated testing on desktop and mobile.

- AI assistance: an AI assistant (Claude) helped write code and text; AI-generated illustrations are labelled on the site.

HOW IT IS CREATIVE

- "Watch the Sun circle the horizon": an animation of the real 30-day path of the Sun around the real skyline of Shackleton rim.

- A 360° panorama for every site, showing the Sun and Earth over the real hills.

- "Nearest spot that sees Earth" turns a "this site is bad for radio" answer into a concrete suggestion: how far to move, in which direction, and whether the slope is gentle enough for a rover.

- The same tool serves two audiences: Beginner mode for the public, Expert mode for engineers.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

- Accuracy: we validated our results against JPL Horizons and between our Python and JavaScript code (less than 0.1% difference). Custom points use the coarser 240 m terrain and are less precise than the 23 pre-computed sites; we say so on the site.

- Energy: solar power assumes a 30% efficient panel facing the Sun.

- Communication: we model direct line of sight to Earth only, not relay satellites.

- Accessibility: plain language, light and dark mode, mobile layout and reduced motion support.

- Performance: compact binary data so everything loads fast, even on a phone.
